commenti.body: I think 'Best Lists' are pretty stupid, it's just like making a  list of 'best music'. There are so many tastes that making an universal list is impossible so these lists become popularity contests. On the other hand I love lists because it exposes me to films I would possibly miss, when I dive in to Sight&Sound list I know I'll be having a good time. The same applies to music, I find a lot of artists through publications because I trust my sources.

Personally, I think all those rankings are mere **popularity** rankings and nothing more. The IMDB one is particularly laughable, it's such a snapshot of a certain demographic at a certain time... but as a measure of "objective value" (whatever that means)? Eh, no, nothing of the kind (in my opinion). Don't get me wrong--I don't hate on them, I think it's mostly harmless fun, and sure, I could come up with a list (unordered) of my 100 or 10 faves... but I couldn't seriously expect anyone else to agree.

I think they're fun, especially the IMDB one. I always enjoyed the years long battle between Shawshank and The Godfather, and it started a long running beef between me and one of my friends after I told them that Shawshank probably wouldn't even make my top 250

I think people just get fascinated with them on the idea that they want to understand if the person or sponsored thing has a similar taste to them and can use the listing to help find new titles they may like and enjoy. Because the only 2 reactions to them ever seem to be people bickering about what is missing or overrated or people championing obscure titles they personally enjoy.  Nobody even really acknowledges or cares when a film with a great reputation is listed highly because that's not what they want out of the list. They want surprises and guidance.

I use a website called "icheckmovies.com" to keep track of what movies I've seen. The website has tons of different lists of movies to sort through and check. You can see IMDB's Top 250, Best Picture Oscar Winners, AFI's 100 Years list, Roger Eberts Favorite Films list, etc. There are over 200 official lists to sort through.

Another fun feature is you can sort movies by what lists they appear in. Meaning, it will tell you what movies appear in the most official lists. And it's not a top 100 or 250, it just keeps going and going. For me personally, this is the better metric to finding "the greatest" film, even if it is still subjective. Currently the [top 10 movies](https://www.icheckmovies.com/movies/?sort=officialtoplists) are....

1. 2001: A Space Oddysey (45 Lists)
2. The Godfather (42)
3. Vertigo (42)
4. Lawrence of Arabia (40)
5. Star Wars (40)
6. Casablanca (39)
7. Citizen Kane (39)
8. Psycho (39)
9. Spirited Away (39)
10. Pulp Fiction (38)
11. The Wizard of Oz (38)

Your text is a bit long too read, maybe top 250 words would cover what you are trying to say? Kidding, kind of. 

I like top 100, top 250, top 1000 lists. I see them as encyclopaedias of possibilities, it’s not a canon or bible or anything like that, it’s a list that someone put together lovingly of the best films they’ve seen presumably of many more. My partner has a great list of films where he puts every single film he sees in his list and top 250 are obviously best ranked. And top 100. And top 10. He’s a film writer but also film nerd/cinephile like me. I can give you my top 10 or top 20 but them my record keeping fails me, although with a help of other people’s lists I could create my own top 100. It’s really just a cinephile map, when I see someone’s list that aligns with mine I get really excited about the films on their list I haven’t seen. I get super excited about directors I’ve never heard of (because I know and have seen 90% of Sight and Sound kinds of lists), so lists are exciting for me to discover something new. I don’t care about rankings one bit, it’s all subjective.

IMDBs top 100 was my gateway to appreciating movies and finding what I like and what I don’t like. Having lists of movies that have certain qualities enables me to keep my own lists on what to or not to waste my time on. It is a crucial system that easily beats any suggestion system I tried and keeps me away from being a prisoner of streaming services.

They are not stupid, they are way to organise favourite films and keep track of them for those who are into film. But they should not get taken literally as “best films of all time”, they are best in that person’s opinion;)

I disagree with the word stupid as it's quite strong, but I still find ranked lists to be a hindrance to genuine discourse.

Too many instances of any artistic consumption is like comparing apples to oranges, whether it's books, music, exhibitions or film.

How can one compare the soft cuddly enjoyment of a guilty pleasure or Sunday morning favourite with the dramatic rigour of a plus-sized and cerebral "world cinema" experience?

If I say that Unbreakable is my "number one" film, and then "Werckmeister Harmonies" my number two, what conversation does that generate between the two films? Or does the conversation merely become about myself and my tastes (which I don't think is the purpose of art to elucidate.)

Worst yet, if I consistently asterisk my "list"/"rankings" with the provision that it depends on my mood, the weather, and/or the height of the sun in the sky, then it becomes less and less of a tangible leaping off point.

People should talk about their enjoyment of films, they should discuss how and why they worked for them individually, but I don't ever bother with ranking.

I think GOAT lists are important in that they're a way we collectively define our notion of quality in art, and thereby define ourselves. 

Art is not just something an individual produces in order than a different individual can look at and like or dislike and that's the end of the story. Art is a way we invent who we are, both as individuals and as a society (if indeed there is a difference). 

Some films become popular and for a while become part of who we are. They become a conversation we have with each other and they contribute to who we are. Some films are elevated beyond this level. They become iconic. These tend to be films (Godfather, 2001, Seventh Seal, Seven Samurai etc) we revere, almost as if they were Gods among films. To state bluntly "*The Godfather is over rated"* has an air of blasphemy about it. Critics 'best ever' lists are possibly the principle way we create these icons (the 'canon'). They are an important focal point in the constantly evolving effort to define quality in art. 

The canon provides the illusion of permanence, as if it's set in stone. But at the same time we know it's not permanent, and every now and then one of the revered icons is ejected from the list, and a new icon is tried out. So there's a constant underlying tension to these lists. They bother people, and the people they bother tend to be those who are engaged in defining who they are and defining their society (again, if there is any difference between these two). The tension, so well expressed in the regular posts on this sub about the value or otherwise of lists, is a vital, ongoing conversation that contributes to our human identity. The lists are essential to this project, as are conversations about their relevance and value. What I'm saying is that nothing's broken here.
